sites.evidence_type: published tag insertion in the same loop or domain
sites.functional_impact_measured: Immunofluorescence confirmed cell-surface membrane expression; NPS-induced signalling was comparable to untagged NPSR1 (data shown in PMC3244468).
sites.rationale: L1–L4 all describe 'N-terminal Myc-tagged full-length NPSR1' expressed as a membrane-anchored receptor. NPSR1 has no signal peptide (topology string begins with O at residue 1), so the N-terminus is extracellular and there is exactly one extracellular N-terminal position: a prepend before residue 1 (insert_after_residue=0, residue_after=M). No specific residue number is cited in the papers, so position_evidence is topology_derived. Python confirmed residue 1 = M and that the topology is O from position 1, with TM1 beginning at residue 53, leaving 52 extracellular residues between the tag and the first TM helix. Full-length NPSR1 cDNA with an N-terminal Myc tag expressed in HEK293 cells; immunofluorescence confirmed membrane localisation; NPS-induced signalling was compared to untagged receptor.

sources.claim: HEK293 cells were transfected with N-terminal Myc-tagged NPSR1 cDNA expression vectors corresponding to different coding variants.

literature_notes: L5, L6, and L7 (PMC4116602) describe full-length NPSR1-A-pDsRed, NPSR1-B-GFP, and NPSR1-A-GFP fusions. The naming convention 'NPSR1-X-FP' indicates C-terminal fusions. The NPSR1 C-terminus (residues 333–371) is intracellular per the authoritative topology landmarks; these constructs therefore carry an intracellular fluorescent-protein tag and do not qualify as extracellular surface-tag sites. They are recorded in other_positions. L1–L4 are four clips from the same paper (PMC3244468) all describing the same N-terminal Myc-tagged construct; they ground a single site, not four separate sites.

literature_other_positions.note: NPSR1-A-pDsRed and NPSR1-B-GFP fusions (C-terminal FP) expressed in COS-7 and SH-SY5Y cells; the NPSR1 C-terminus (residues 333–371) is intracellular, so these fusions label the cytoplasmic face, not the extracellular surface.
